opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is just that citations are so easy to check, and they're checkable in a very binary way. If a model gives you a fuzzy summary of some area of research, it's hard to say it's flat-out wrong. But if it tells you there's a 2017 paper by so-and-so in such-and-such a journal with this exact title, you can go look, and either it exists or it doesn't. Researchers do that kind of lookup all the time, so they hit these fabrications constantly.

The other thing is that a citation is almost a worst case for how these models work. A language model is learning the statistical texture of text, and citations have a very strong, regular texture. There are author names that sound right for a field, title phrasing that sounds like the kind of paper that would exist, plausible venues and years. So the model can produce something that's stylistically perfect and completely fictional. It's a crisp example of the gap between plausibility and truth. The model is very good at "this looks like a citation" and has no built-in notion of "this citation refers to a real object in the world."

And I think there's an emotional component for academics too. Citations are the currency of our profession. They're how we assign credit and build on each other's work. So when a model invents a paper, sometimes attributing it to a real person, maybe even you, it feels like a violation of something we care about, not just an error. That's why it's become the go-to anecdote when people talk about hallucination.

To be fair, things have improved a lot, especially once models are hooked up to retrieval and search and can ground references in actual documents. But the example has stuck because it illustrates the core issue so clearly: fluency isn't the same as faithfulness to facts.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think citations are almost the perfect storm for this kind of failure, and it's worth unpacking why. If you think about what these models are actually doing, they're producing text that's statistically plausible given everything they've seen. And a citation has an extremely regular structure. There's an author list, a title, a venue, a year, maybe a page range. The model has seen millions of these, so it's very, very good at generating something that looks exactly like a citation. The surface form is easy to get right.

The problem is that a citation is also one of the most tightly constrained objects you can ask for. It's not enough to be plausible. It has to point to a specific document that actually exists, with those exact authors, in that exact venue, in that exact year. So you have this enormous gap between how easy it is to produce the form and how hard it is to produce the content. The model will happily combine a real author who works in the area, a title that sounds like something that person would have written, and a conference where that kind of work gets published, and stitch them together into something that has never existed. And it does it with complete fluency.

The other thing that makes it so notorious among researchers specifically is that we're the ones who check. Most people reading a chatbot's answer about history or cooking aren't going to go verify it. But if you hand a researcher a reference list, the first thing they do is go look up the papers. So the hallucination gets caught immediately and very publicly. Everyone in the field has a story of asking for references on some topic and getting back five papers where two are real, one is a real title with the wrong authors, and two are pure fabrication. That's a very visceral experience, and it travels fast.

And I'd add that it cuts at something researchers care about deeply, which is provenance. The whole scientific enterprise rests on being able to trace a claim back to its source. A fake citation isn't just a wrong fact, it's a corruption of the mechanism we use to establish what's true. So it's not surprising it became the canonical example. It's the case where the failure mode is easiest to demonstrate, hardest to excuse, and most offensive to the people most likely to notice it.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think citations are a particularly striking example because researchers know what a citation is supposed to do. It’s supposed to point you to an actual piece of evidence that you can go and inspect. And a language model can produce something that has all the surface features of a perfectly reasonable citation—the right authors, a plausible title, an appropriate journal—without that paper existing at all.

So there’s this very sharp distinction between plausibility and truth. If you ask about a topic you know well, you might recognize the authors and think, “Oh, I didn’t know they wrote a paper together.” Then you go looking for it, and it isn’t there. The specificity makes it seem authoritative, but that specificity isn’t a guarantee that anything was verified.

And for researchers, that hits directly at how we work. A fabricated citation isn’t just an incorrect detail; it breaks the connection between a claim and the evidence that’s supposed to support it.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think citations are a particularly striking example because they have this veneer of precision and authority. You get a title, a list of authors, a venue, a year—all the things that make something look like a real scholarly reference. And then you go looking for it, and it doesn’t exist.

The model is very good at producing something that looks like a citation. But that’s a different task from identifying a paper that actually exists and supports the claim being made. And researchers are especially sensitive to that distinction, because citations are how we check each other’s work. A fabricated reference breaks that chain of verification, even if the surrounding prose sounds perfectly plausible.
